about: What a balance pass is allowed to change about each spell, and what each spell is for. Read data/balance/README.md before editing. This file is authoring metadata: the data builder never reads it, so it does not touch the content hash.

objective.confirm: The seeds a tuning pass confirms a new leader on (ADR 0074): 400 seeds from 2000000, clear of the benchmark seeds and of the 200 above them the hold-out replays on. A round's best candidate is chosen on the benchmark seeds out of every candidate of the round, so its score there is the best of several noisy readings and flatters it; it takes the lead only if it also beats the leader here, where it was not chosen. The objective at 200 seeds moves 2.6 from one seed block to the next on the same content, and a single move measured neutral at 200 seeds read 2.4 worse at 800. This changes which candidate a pass keeps, never the score a candidate gets.

mirror.reads: Both sides play the content equally well, so everything left is the content: how long a match lasts, how often it is drawn or capped, how often a declaration fizzles. Not who wins it -- two identical deterministic agents on a symmetric board buy the same packages in the same rounds, tie on every initiative and hand the tie to the seat, so the seat question is read on variety instead (ADR 0062).

skill.reads: Playing well still beats playing at random. A change that closes this gap has removed the decisions instead of balancing them.

variety.reads: Whether the content offers a choice, which is a different question from whether a greedy bot takes one. Both sides play greedily four decisions in five and draw uniformly the fifth (ADR 0014), so a spell the argmax always passes over still gets cast and can be read. Every target that needs a spell to be cast in order to mean anything is read here rather than on the mirrored run.

exploit.reads: How far a player who only wants to win gets against the way the game is meant to be played. Greedy is the taste this catalogue is balanced for; agent A is a searched set that shares none of it and beats Greedy anyway. Content where the two are far apart is content that punishes playing it the intended way. Agent A is a panel and the reading is its best exploiter (ADR 0052): one agent only ever reads what that agent happens to punish, and the same one-spell move was worth 0.013 to one of these sets and 0.235 to another (journal, 2026-09-17), so the term named a pair rather than a catalogue. Every set is played and the highest win rate decides the evaluation. A set goes stale when the content moves — a tuning pass changes what there is to exploit — so the newest search joins the panel rather than replacing it, and an older set stays because a moved catalogue sometimes blinds the newer ones and not it. kill-first is the one set searched on a catalogue other than this one, the weakened Crushing Stomp of that same entry, and it takes every match on both: a set fitted to a moved catalogue finds another route rather than losing the old one, which is why this term is a constant this file cannot spend content on (journal, 2026-09-17). So what is scored here is no longer whether the best exploiter wins but how fast it does (ADR 0053), and a tie at the top of the panel goes to the fastest win rather than to the first name in the list. On 2026-09-24 the panel was measured again under the stun immunity, the bleed price and the defense ceiling (ADR 0072, 0073, 0076) on the benchmark seeds: search-4, mixture-mean, search-2, search-3 and mixture-worst no longer beat Greedy (0.44 to 0.50), so none of them can be the best exploiter and they left; search-23 and search-21 take every match and joined; kill-first (0.806) left as the weakest of the six that still beat Greedy, so the panel stays at five evaluations a candidate. On 2026-09-29 it was measured again under ADR 0083 to 0085: search-23 fell to 0.196 against Greedy and left; kill-first came back at 0.995, the second best after search-19 (1.000); lookahead-30 (0.975, 13.37 rounds), the newest search, joined, because a moved catalogue can make it the best exploiter where search-19 is today; and stun-first (0.710) left as the weakest of the sets that still beat Greedy, so the panel stays at five evaluations a candidate. Tuning pass 14 then ran out of its six hours inside its opening sweep: a candidate cost 117 seconds on the runner against the 61.7 tune.yml is sized for, and lookahead-30 alone was 77 of the 190 seconds its eight evaluations take one after another. So lookahead-30 left again and stun-first came back: the panel's rule keeps the newest search in only when a pass can afford to play it, and a pass that cannot finish reads nothing at all. On content 9659f610 (2026-09-30) search-31, the newest search, joined: it takes every match from Greedy in 12.28 rounds; stun-first left again as the weakest set that still beats Greedy (0.740), so a candidate still costs five exploit evaluations. search-19 remains the best exploiter, at 1.000 in 12.18 rounds.

objective.score: Sum over the targets of weight * (distance outside the band / scale) ** 2. Zero is on target, lower is better. Metric names are report.json's, so a target and a report row are the same number; spellUsageShare, spellsNeverCast and spellsBarelyCast are the ones the tuner adds, because they need the catalogue and not only the evaluation. A candidate that breaks a constraint is not scored at all. Adding spellsBarelyCast made every score before it incomparable with every score after it: a run reading 40.45 under the old set is not a better run than one reading 41 under this one. ADR 0029 did it again, and harder: seven targets moved off the mirrored run onto the exploring one without their bands changing, which took the core content from 69.39 to 52.00 without a single number in the content moving. ADR 0062 did it a third time: player1WinShare moved from the mirror to the exploring run, which took the shipped content from 285.77 to 42.77 with the content unchanged. ADR 0064 did it a fourth time: tierUsageShare reads the lower Wilson bound of a package's top share against a band of 0.8, not the raw share against the even split every package's floor sits at. ADR 0065 did it a fifth: tierWinSpread reads the lower Newcombe bound of a package's win gap, not the raw gap. ADR 0068 did it a sixth: the mirror's rounds band moved from 8-16 to 10-15 and the exploit floor from 8 to 10, the length the game is designed for. ADR 0071 did it a seventh: that band moved from the mirror to the exploring run. Refreshing the exploit panel on 2026-09-24 did it a sixth time, and again on 2026-09-29: the evaluation reads other agents. ADR 0090 did it again: `tierDamageSpread` left the targets, because a raw ratio of hits per target cannot see a spell's cost, reach or riders, and the three packages it held outside its band were each split that way on purpose; it is still reported. Compare scores only across runs judged by the same set read from the same runs.

targets.why: Equal skill on both sides, so anything away from one half is the content favouring a slot. Read on the exploring run since ADR 0062, for the reason ADR 0029 moved seven targets there: on the greedy mirror under packages both sides buy the same package in the same round, every initiative ties, and the seat breaks the tie -- Player 1 took 400 of 400 on four catalogues in five, so the reading measured the tie-break rule and not the content, and was 243 of an objective of 285.77. On the exploring run the two sides diverge and the question has an answer: 0.44 to 0.495 on the same five catalogues.
A draw is the round cap arriving before either team can finish the other.

The length the game is designed for: eight to fourteen rounds (ADR 0086, which moved it from ADR 0068's ten to fifteen). Long enough that a bad round can be traded back and the deepest packages, which arrive at round 5 at the earliest since ADR 0066, get played; short enough that the cap of 30 stays out of reach. Read on the exploring run, not the greedy mirror (ADR 0071): two greedy agents play a narrow game that ends sooner than a person's would, and a band on the mirror held every tuning pass at its bottom edge, where any move that shortened the mirror by a tenth of a round was penalised however it played. The mirror read 7.8 at 20 base health under ADR 0066 and 10.05 at 30; the exploring run reads 10.03 at 30, and 9.9 to 10.2 on ab944cfb, which is what ADR 0086 lowered the band from the bottom edge of.
Matches that run out of rounds mean neither side can convert, usually stacked permanent defense.

Agent A's share of declarations that fizzled. Both agents are the same in a mirrored run, so A is the content's own rate. Mostly targets dying before the action resolves, so it falls on its own as matches lengthen. 21.4% at the last measured run.

Bits over agent A's declared spells. 2.21 at the last measured run over ten distinct spells, of a possible 5.17 over thirty-six. Read on the exploring run (ADR 0029), where it reads 2.530 against 1.992 on a mirrored greedy run: the difference was the argmax passing spells over, not the content failing to offer them.

The largest share of landed casts any one spell takes across the whole catalogue. Since tierUsageShare reads the same thing inside each package and catches what this one hides — a package whose casts all go to one of its spells, small in the total — this stays as the coarse guard and carries half the weight. 0.855 on the core content. Read on the exploring run (ADR 0029), where it reads 0.410 against 0.478 on a mirrored greedy run: the difference was the argmax passing spells over, not the content failing to offer them.

Spells in the catalogue that no declaration ever landed. Needs the catalogue as well as the evaluation, so the tuner computes it. The band is read against what the build carries, not against what is on disk: on the nine-spell core content two spells failing to come up is slack, twelve would be the whole game. Read on the exploring run (ADR 0029), where it reads 0 against 2 on a mirrored greedy run: the difference was the argmax passing spells over, not the content failing to offer them.

Spells taking under 1% of the landed casts of the package that teaches them. The hole spellsNeverCast leaves: pummel took 6 of 5283 landed casts of a mirrored run, which is dead in every sense that decides a game and is not a zero, so a buff that moved it from 4 casts to 6 read as no change at all. Read against the package rather than the catalogue because the package is what one pick buys (ADR 0058): a spell can be rare overall and still be worth the pick that brought it, and a package carrying one spell nobody casts sold that pick short. A spell several packages teach is read against each and counted once. Counts strictly the spells spellsNeverCast does not: a zero is a zero in either reading, and with the same band and weight on both, counting it twice would quietly double what the objective asks of that one case. A run whose content carries no packages reports this as missing rather than as zero. Read on the exploring run (ADR 0029), where it reads 0 against 1 on a mirrored greedy run: the difference was the argmax passing spells over, not the content failing to offer them.

Whether every spell of a package earns part of the pick that bought it (ADR 0058): the share of a package's landed casts its most-cast spell takes, worst package, read as the lower bound of its 95 % Wilson interval (ADR 0064). A package teaching one spell is skipped: it takes all of its own casts whatever the content does. The band is not an even split. Every package that teaches more than one spell teaches two, so 0.5 was the floor of each and the band demanded a perfect split from all eleven at once; a catalogue whose every pair truly splits evenly read 0.667 raw at the median, from sampling alone, and paid 5.6 points no move could remove. Spells sold together must differ in play (ADR 0060), and a heal beside an attack is not cast half the time. What the band refuses is the spell that came along for nothing: 0.8 is the other spell taking at least one cast in five, as far as the sample shows. On the shipped catalogue `tier:soulreaver:v1` reads 0.899 (267 of 286), `tier:deathstalker:v1` 0.861 and `tier:prowler:v1` 0.840. Read on the exploring run (ADR 0029): a greedy argmax monopolises a pair on any numbers.

The gap between two win shares among the spells of one package, worst package, counting only spells enough sides declared, read as the lower bound of the 95 % Newcombe interval of the difference (ADR 0065). Two spells bought by the same pick should not be worth wildly different results. Read raw it was mostly the size of the samples: a catalogue whose every pair truly wins alike read a worst gap of 0.254 at the median and 0.399 at the 90th percentile on the sides the exploring run gives each package, so the tuner was scoring 1 to 6 points of chance. The bound reads 0 for a gap its sides cannot tell from chance, and a gap they prove close to itself: `tier:blightweaver:v1` wins 0.659 of 22 sides with `tranquilizer_dart` and 0.148 of 27 with `infectious_blast`, 0.511 raw and 0.238 bounded. Read on the exploring run (ADR 0029), where it read 0.148 against 0.322 raw on a mirrored greedy run: the difference was the argmax passing spells over, not the content failing to offer them.
The skill gap. Content that a random agent can hold has stopped asking anything.

Played and reported, not scored (ADR 0053). It is the gate that decides which member of the panel the reading comes from, and it stopped scoring because it is pinned at its ceiling: every catalogue measured reads 1.000 against Greedy once a set is searched against it, three of the five panel members read 1.000 on this one, and the one-spell move that a single agent priced at 116 points of objective is worth nothing at all to a set fitted to the catalogue it faces (journal, 2026-09-17). At weight 2 it was 162.00 of the 172.42 points this content scored, 94 % of an objective it could not move: an offset rather than a target, and the offset ADR 0044 froze content tuning over. Turning the opponent up closes the other end rather than opening this one -- against stun-first the same panel reads 0.175 down to 0.005 -- so there is no room further along this axis either. As a diagnostic it still says something: below 1.000 it names the panel members the content still holds, and its own history is a record of stale agents (0.5875 on d4a21a55, 0.8075 on 938bef5e, 0.9275 on 7e199df4 with search-4) rather than of safe catalogues.

How fast the best exploiter closes it out, which is what the win rate stopped being able to say (ADR 0053). Eight rounds is the floor a match is held to (ADR 0086; ADR 0068 had raised it from eight to ten), read on the exploring run since ADR 0071, so this reads: the catalogue should not let a player who only wants to win end it faster than a fair game is expected to last. It reads 5.785 on 7e199df4 for 2.45 of a 12.87 objective, and 7.553 for 0.10 with Crushing Stomp at the weakest of its own bounds, where the win rate reads 1.000 and 162.00 on both, to the decimal. So this is the axis a content move actually travels, and both readings are this panel's, scored the way a tuning pass scores a candidate rather than by fitting a fresh agent to each catalogue. The scale is two rounds, about what one spell's worth of pressure moves it. A clock can be gamed by making every match longer, and what stands against that is the exploring run's own 8-to-14 band and the variety spreads; if a pass starts buying rounds rather than balance, this target needs an upper band too.

noNewStrictDominance.what: A candidate may not add a pair where one spell is strictly better than another: same targeting origin, at least as many targets, cost no higher, critical chance no lower, every effect at least as large, and strictly better on one of them.
noNewStrictDominance.why: A spell three nodes down the tree outclassing a starting spell is what progression means, so the pairs the catalogue already has are not defects to remove. Adding one is: it takes a decision out of a hand that had it. Journal entry ci-9 spent a whole learning investigation discovering the starting kit was shaped that way.

noIndistinguishableSpells.what: No two spells may carry the same cost, critical chance, targeting and effects. The same signature the engine's Spell.Indistinguishable audit compares.
noIndistinguishableSpells.why: The engine plays both, but no result can attribute anything to either, so tuning one moves nothing the other does not.

startingKitOffersAChoice.what: None of the three spells every creature starts with may be strictly better than another. Implied by noNewStrictDominance, named separately because this is the one hand every match is dealt.
startingKitOffersAChoice.why: Journal entry ci-9: heavy_strike was strictly better than basic_attack, and no learner could find a decision that was not there.

spell:wait.name: Wait
spell:wait.intent: The floor of the game: spend the activation on nothing and come back two energy richer. It is what a creature does when everything it knows is too expensive, so it must stay free and it must stay worse than acting.
keep: Free to cast
Never worth more than an attack the creature can already afford

spell:basic_attack.name: Basic Attack
spell:basic_attack.intent: The reliable jab of the starting kit: cheap, certain, no critical. Every other attack in the catalogue is priced against its damage per energy, so moving it moves everything.
keep: The cheapest damaging spell a creature knows on round one
No critical chance: it is the predictable one

spell:heavy_strike.name: Heavy Strike
spell:heavy_strike.intent: The starting kit's commitment: pay more of the round for the bigger opening hit. The decision it exists to pose is spend now or bank for later, so it has to cost what it wins.
keep: Strictly dearer and stronger than Basic Attack, never both cheaper and better
The reason a first round has a choice in it

spell:pummel.name: Pummel
spell:pummel.intent: The Brawler's cheap swing: one energy for a hit that crits about three times in four. It buys tempo rather than a big number, and the critical chance is the whole reason to take it over Basic Attack.
keep: At most one energy dearer than Basic Attack
Its critical chance stays its defining stat
spell:pummel.note: check-knobs reports this spell as outclassed, and raising its own bounds is not the way out. At 4 damage it would be strictly better than Lightning Bolt -- same damage, a higher critical chance (0.767 against 0.5), one energy cheaper -- so noNewStrictDominance refuses it, and a wider bound here would only buy candidates the constraints throw away. Measured: its whole box tops out around 5.4 against Lightning Bolt's 6.0, and even a certain critical at 3 damage only reaches 6.0, a tie. Its other edge, costing 1 against 2, is worth nothing on this rule set: 0 of 319 traced declarations had the caster below 2 energy, so the cost never binds. Making this spell a choice is a move on the pair -- Lightning Bolt down as this one comes up -- which is a two-spell candidate, so neither the sweep nor the paired opening can build it and only the climb can. That is what the search budget is for.

spell:guard.name: Guard
spell:guard.intent: The Brawler's investment: a point of defense on an ally for good, plus a point while the pressure is on. Cheap, repeatable and permanent, which makes it the likeliest single cause of a match no one can finish.
keep: Half of it is permanent and stacks on every cast
No dearer than any heal: it prevents, it does not repair

spell:extort.name: Extort
spell:extort.intent: The Mercenary takes its cut: a cheap hit that skims a point of energy off the target and pockets one. It slows an enemy's big spells without ever locking them, which is the whole design: the drain stays under the two a creature earns each round, so the target always climbs, and the price stays at or above what the caster pockets, so casting it every round banks nothing.
keep: Never a lock: the drain stays below the energy a creature earns each round
Never a farm: the energy cost stays at or above the energy the caster gains
A hit first: the damage is what makes it worth the activation, the skim is the flavour
spell:extort.note: Authored at 4.5 a round in the check-knobs reading, the bottom of the tier-2 attacks but for Momentum's 2.6, because that reading prices energy at 0.3 and cannot see a big spell pushed back a round. No evaluation has measured it yet.

spell:protective_slam.name: Protective Slam
spell:protective_slam.intent: The Mercenary's opener, and the branch's answer to armour. Legacy gave its caster a point of defense; a caster effect can say that now, as Shield Bash's brace does, but on this spell armour would break the Mercenary's line, so it stays off. Protection is expressed as tempo instead -- a slammed enemy acts later -- which is the one protective thing that can be said to an enemy. That also gives it teeth a bigger hit would not have: defense absorbs damage and does nothing to a stagger, so this is what a Brawler stacking Guard and Full Plate is answered with.
keep: Protection through tempo, never armour: it always carries an initiative debuff
Reads as a trade, not a nuke
The stagger is the point; the damage only has to be worth the activation
spell:protective_slam.note: Most of its value was damage on purpose, because the initiative weight was 0.5 on reasoning alone (ADR 0018) and a version built mainly on the debuff would have rested on an unmeasured number. That objection is now spent: ADR 0032 swept the weight alone and moved it to 2.1, and the debuff half of this spell is what moved with it -- 1.6% of the mirror's casts to 7.0%, without a number here changing. The shape is worth revisiting deliberately rather than by default: at 2.1 the debuff is no longer the cheap half.

spell:chain_slash.name: Chain Slash
spell:chain_slash.intent: The Mercenary's payoff, and, beside Throwing Star, the only cast in the catalogue that hits exactly two, and the harder of the pair: the rung between a single-target spike and a line-wide storm. It is the reason to walk that line to the end, so it stays expensive and stays late.
keep: Hits exactly two: the rung between a spike and a storm, shared only with `throwing_star` at tier 1, which it outhits
Expensive and late: the end of the Mercenary's line, never something to open with
spell:chain_slash.note: It used to claim to be 'the largest cast in the catalogue', which was true only while the spells that beat it were disabled. It puts 10 damage on the board, 5 over two targets; `crazed_specter` puts 18 and `tornado` 15, both at the same depth, `hateful_sacrifice` beats it at 11 on one, and `engulfing_flames` and `psycho_rush` tie it at 10 on one. Its numbers are not the problem and were left alone: at 10.00 a round it already sits inside the 8-to-14 band tier 3 is being aimed at, and two candidates that made it bigger -- damage 6 at a cost of 4, and damage 6 at a critical chance of 0.6 -- both measured worse than what is authored. What was wrong was the sentence.

spell:thundering_seal.name: Thundering Seal
spell:thundering_seal.intent: Guard grown up: three permanent points of defense on an ally and three more for two rounds. The damage it used to send back to the attacker was not carried over (ADR 0012), so what is left is pure stacking mitigation. It is the one place the Mercenary protects with armour rather than with tempo -- `protective_slam` says 'never armour' and means it -- because the taxonomy's initiative buff (ADR 0036) belongs to the Assassin's line, not to this one, so the Mercenary protects an ally with armour alone.
keep: Stronger and dearer than Guard
The permanent half stacks on every cast
spell:thundering_seal.note: It read 5.20 a round against a tier-3 band of 8 to 14, so it was raised to the top of its own bounds rather than redesigned: 2 permanent and 2 for a round became 3 and 3 for two, at the same price. Measured, that is 16 casts to 94 and `spellsNeverCast` 6 to 1 -- longer matches (5.56 rounds to 6.33) buy more evolution picks, so more of the catalogue comes up at all. It is not the best score available: 3 permanent and 2 for two rounds reads 34.33 against this one's 39.97, and the difference is `spellsBarelyCast`. Taken deliberately, because the tier's problem is its floor and this is the shape closer to the tier-3 median, about 10.5 then and about 9.4 today. Its overlap with `revenant_guards` -- the same two effects on three allies -- is left for the Necromancer's turn.

spell:shield_bash.name: Shield Bash
spell:shield_bash.intent: Ironbound's active answer: Full Plate only armours its caster, so without this the package bought nothing to hit with until Dreadnought. A hit that leaves the caster braced keeps the Warlord's armour identity while giving the tier-2 pick a move of its own, priced beside Enraged Charge and Protective Slam at three energy.
keep: Always an attack that also armours its caster, never pure armour: self-defense alone is what Full Plate already sells
A tier-2 price, beside the Berserker and Marauder openers rather than above them
spell:shield_bash.note: Authored at 8.4 a round in the check-knobs reading, the same as Enraged Charge; no evaluation has measured it yet.

spell:full_plate.name: Full Plate
spell:full_plate.intent: Armour the Warlord is meant to always wear. Nothing implements passives yet, so it is three self-targeted permanent points of defense that can be cast every single round, and permanent plus repeatable is only bounded by what it costs. It costs one energy for that reason: half a round's income for three points, so a creature that armours itself is a creature not attacking, which is the trade the spell should be.
keep: Plate, not a shirt: one cast is armour a creature can feel, and it stacks by being cast again
Never free: a permanent effect nobody pays for has no brake but the round cap
Cheap enough to cast in the rounds that decide the match, or it is not armour
spell:full_plate.note: Its price is the whole design and the reason its lower bound is one rather than zero. The spell is `SpellType.Passive` in a model where nothing implements a passive, so it is castable, repeatable and permanent; at zero it was unbounded and read 0.65 against the bolt's 6.47, which is how it went 400 matches without a single cast while being the most dangerous spell in the catalogue. Raising the permanent horizon would not have found that -- every reading prices one cast, and one point of defense is one point at any horizon. When a passive becomes a real always-on modifier, this entry is the first to revisit. It is also half of the Warlord's opener, Ironbound, beside Shield Bash, so `restorative_gush` and `crushing_stomp` are only ever as reachable as that package is. At 2 permanent it was declared by 5 sides of 400 on the mirrored run and both children were cast zero times -- a branch nobody walked, whose numbers could not be measured because nobody arrived to use them. At 3 it is declared by 34 and the two behind it are cast 26 and 55. Raising it was the only way to learn anything about the two spells this pass was about.

spell:restorative_gush.name: Restorative Gush
spell:restorative_gush.intent: The big single-target heal: more health back than most single hits take away. It decides on its own whether a war of attrition is winnable, which is why the average match length moves with it.
keep: Heals more at once on one ally than anything else
Single target: the team heals belong to the Trickster and the Shaman
spell:restorative_gush.note: Its critical chance became a live number with ADR 0033, and that ADR's follow-up said the knob was added here. It was not -- this entry carried three sentences that were false by the time anyone read them: that the knob existed, that the spell was disabled, and that it carried no chance. The knob is real now. The heal goes to 7 with a chance of 0.5, which is 5.62 a round to 8.40 and inside the 8-to-14 band tier 3 is aimed at; its own bounds could not reach the band on the heal alone, which is why the missing knob mattered rather than being a tidy-up.

spell:crushing_stomp.name: Crushing Stomp
spell:crushing_stomp.intent: The Warlord's hammer and the costliest spell in the game: heavy damage and two rounds of the target doing nothing. Losing an activation is the harshest thing that can happen to a creature, so the price is the point of the spell.
keep: The most expensive cast in the catalogue
Damage and stun together, or it is just an expensive hit
spell:crushing_stomp.note: Raised inside its own bounds to reach its tier: damage 6 to 7, chance 0.667 to 0.8, and the stun from one round to two, all at the same price of 4. That is 6.50 a round to 9.30. The price did not move because the price is the spell -- it is the most expensive cast in the catalogue and that is the first thing its entry keeps. Two rounds of a creature doing nothing is the harshest thing in the game, and it costs two rounds of income to say it. Its chance then came back down from 0.8 to 0.75, one round after it went up: at 0.8 it tied `enraged_charge`, whose entry keeps 'the highest critical chance in the catalogue' as the thing that makes it a Berserker spell rather than an expensive hit. Nothing this spell keeps mentions its chance, so the tie cost the other class its identity and cost this one nothing -- 9.30 a round to 9.12.

spell:reckless_swing.name: Reckless Swing
spell:reckless_swing.intent: The Berserker's every-round swing: cheap enough to throw each round on the income alone, and paid for in the Berserker's own blood. Enraged Charge is the big hit two rounds in three; this is what the rage does in between, and the self-inflicted wound is the rage -- the line that ends in Psycho Rush fights by giving something up.
keep: Always hurts its caster: the recklessness is the spell
Cheaper than Enraged Charge and lighter than it, so the Charge stays the finisher
spell:reckless_swing.note: Authored at 5.5 a round in the check-knobs reading, the caster's damage priced as a cost. No evaluation has measured it yet.

spell:enraged_charge.name: Enraged Charge
spell:enraged_charge.intent: The Berserker's gamble, and the one spell in the catalogue whose whole point is the roll. One heavy swing at the highest critical chance anywhere, bought at a price that keeps it to two rounds in three: rage that lands or does not, rather than a steady beat. It comes in one package with Reckless Swing, the every-round beat, so the class is offered the gamble and the steady hit together.
keep: One swing, not a flurry: the roll is the spell, and two effects only split it
The highest critical chance in the catalogue, or it is just an expensive hit
Expensive enough that it cannot be the every-round attack
spell:enraged_charge.note: It reads big per cast on purpose and must be read per round instead: at three energy against an income of two it comes up two rounds in three, so 12.60 a cast is 8.40 a round against `protective_slam`'s 9.02, also at three energy. Read per cast it looks like twice the bolt; read per round it sits just under the Marauder opener and level with `shield_bash`, which is what a tier-2 opener should be. Its own history is the warning: at 7.00 a cast it was 4.67 a round and fell from 122 landed casts to 32 the moment something at two energy arrived.

spell:tornado.name: Tornado
spell:tornado.intent: The sweep: against a full team it is among the best damage per energy anywhere. Its cost is the first place to look when matches end too quickly, and that is where it has been looked.
keep: Hits each target harder than any other sweep that costs its caster nothing: only `crazed_specter` hits harder, and it pays in health
Its efficiency comes from breadth, not from the size of the hit
It hits harder than `meteor` at the same price, or the two are one spell
spell:tornado.note: Its price went 2 to 3, which its own intent nominates: at 15.96 a round against a tier-3 band of 8 to 14 it was the second-largest reading in the catalogue, and matches were ending at 6.4 rounds under a band of 8. At 3 it read 10.64; tune run 9 then took its critical chance 0.33 to 0.38 and #246 its damage 4 to 5, and it reads 13.80 today. The alternative measured -- damage 4 to 3, keeping the price at 2 -- reads 7.01 rounds against this one's 6.55 and is the better number, but it turned the spell into what was then a cheaper `meteor` (3 damage on three targets): the same hit on the same three targets, a tier deeper. A tier-3 spell that copies a tier-2 one is the defect this pass exists to remove, so the better reading lost. The old first keep, 'the cheapest spell that reaches three enemies', had been false since `infectious_blast` was enabled at a cost of one.

spell:psycho_rush.name: Psycho Rush
spell:psycho_rush.intent: The Berserker's all-in: a third of a creature in a single cast, two-thirds on a critical, and the caster stands there open for a round afterwards. It throws itself at one target and the recoil is the spell -- swing that hard and you are not covering yourself.
keep: The line's gamble: big, single target, expensive
It costs its caster defense, not health: the Berserker is not hurt by its own swing, it is exposed by it
spell:psycho_rush.note: The Berserker is the class whose point is the roll -- `enraged_charge` carries the highest critical chance in the catalogue and says so in its own first line -- and neither spell behind it gambled at all: both sat at 0.33, below the opener. This one now takes 0.5, the top of its own bounds, with the damage at 10: 7.98 a round to 10.00, inside the tier-3 band. Measured, 6 casts to 53. Its second keep used to read 'priced as if the recoil existed, because one day it will'; that day is ADR 0035, and the recoil is on the spell -- 2 defense off its own caster for a round, which is what legacy wrote and what `casterEffects` was built to carry (ADR 0031). It costs 1.30 of the reading, 10.00 a round to 9.13, and the spell stopped reading as strictly better than `engulfing_flames`: the finding was the missing half, not a bound.

spell:poison_slash.name: Poison Slash
spell:poison_slash.intent: The Scoundrel's signature: a small hit that keeps hurting. It is the first way into bleed, at level 1, and the spell that teaches a player what a lasting effect is.
keep: The bleed is the point, the damage is the garnish
The entry-level bleed: weaker than Mortal Wound on every axis
spell:poison_slash.note: These bounds contain a good answer and it is in the interior, not at a corner -- but the measurements below were taken on the Brawler-buffed catalogue of the studio/content branch, where this spell carries a bleed of 1 per round over 2 rounds and Pummel carries 3 damage. The catalogue then carried 1 over 1 (it has carried 3 damage and 3 over 1 since the 2026-09-12 pass), so read them as the shape of the curve and not as this catalogue's numbers. There, at 2 damage: 1 over 2 is 6 landed casts; 2 over 2 is 59, still nothing; 2 over 3 takes 5155 of about 8900 with matches at 11.3 rounds, no draw and nothing at the round cap; 3 over 2 reaches the same usage with 12.5% draws; and the corner, 3 over 3, is worse than the middle at 2600, because it kills so fast that a match is 6.0 rounds and there are half as many casts to take a share of. The middle point takes the top spell's share of landed casts from 0.778 to 0.578. On that catalogue, at 1 over 1, the same spell was at 3 landed casts, and one same-direction pair of steps landed on 2 over 2, which measured 310 casts of about 6150 -- fifty times better and still not the interior point. Whether the objective keeps that first pair is its own question.

spell:throwing_star.name: Throwing Star
spell:throwing_star.intent: The Prowler's second verb. Its packagemate `poison_slash` concentrates -- one target, hit now and bleeding after -- and this one spreads: the same activation, the same price, across two enemies. A thrown weapon reaching more than one thing it is thrown at is the one shape an opener can carry that the class does not already have, and it is what makes the pick a decision every round rather than a decision once. It used to be the tempo half of the package instead, on two points of Base initiative bought at unlock; the package pays that now and pays it whole (ADR 0059), which left the spell as a smaller copy of its sibling.
keep: Reach is the point: the day it hits one target it is `heavy_strike` with a class on it
Never more targets than `meteor`, which is what a Wizard climbs two levels for
Priced level with `poison_slash`: the choice is the shape of the damage, never what it costs
spell:throwing_star.note: The pair it belongs to was the worst reading in the catalogue. On content `d367db1c` the package split its casts **1813 to 140** -- 93 % to `poison_slash` -- because the two spells did the same thing and one did more of it: identical damage per energy at 3.0, and `poison_slash` taking 6 off a target per activation against 3. Costing 1 was the only edge this spell had, and it is worth nothing here: of **123,592** recorded states where a creature knew it, **1.0 %** sat below 2 energy and 77 % sat at 6 or more. The activation is the scarce thing, not the energy. So the cost went level with its sibling and the reach became the difference, which is a difference the board decides and not the price list. What it must not become is the catalogue's cheap sweep: `meteor` is 3 energy for three targets at level 2, and this is 2 for two at level 1 -- the same energy a target but a smaller reading on each (3.00 against `meteor`'s 3.50), shorter reach, and that ordering is the reason a Wizard still climbs. If a tuning pass ever makes this the better sweep, the finding is about `meteor`. Measured on the benchmark seeds, the split did not balance, it flipped: this spell went from **7 % to 85 %** of the pair's landed casts on `variety`, and one point less damage or one energy more each sends it back to about 10 %. Against a deterministic greedy a pair's usage is a step in its numbers, and the step sits between two integers, so `criticalChance` is here as the continuous lever to walk it with. Tuning it is still to do.

spell:latch.name: Latch
spell:latch.intent: The Parasite attached: a point of blood drawn from one enemy each round and fed back to the caster for as long. Parasite Jab steals in one bite; this steals a little every round, keeping the Prowler's bleed as the line's mechanic and turning it into the caster's healing.
keep: What the target bleeds, the caster regenerates: the two halves stay matched
Small per round: the big steal is Parasite Jab's, and Soul Devourer's at tier 3
spell:latch.note: Authored at 4.8 a round in the check-knobs reading. Bleeds and regenerations stack beside the ones already there, so a Latch cast every round keeps three running on each side -- 3 a round drawn and 3 healed, for one energy a round -- which that reading does not see. The duration is the knob to cut if that is too much (two rounds reads 3.2). On #245's content the confirmation seeds' exploring run split the Parasite's casts 43/35 between its two spells; the stacking has not been measured on its own.

spell:parasite_jab.name: Parasite Jab
spell:parasite_jab.intent: The Leech's opener and the first spell in the catalogue that feeds its caster (ADR 0031): a modest bite that puts some of what it takes back into whoever threw it. It is deliberately a lighter hit than its tier's heavy attacks, and with Latch beside it the line that answers being hurt, so the choice it offers is not how hard to hit but whether you need the health.
keep: It always feeds its caster: the bite is the price of the meal, not the point of it
A worse attack than the tier's attacks: the healing is what it is for
Never more healing than a real heal: it is a bite, not a Restorative Gush
spell:parasite_jab.note: The reading that matters is not in the numbers: `ActionScorer`'s `HealTerms` counts only the health a target is missing, so at full health this spell is worth its damage alone -- 4.35 against `lightning_bolt`'s 6.00 -- and only passes it once its caster has three points to get back. That is lifesteal's whole feel, and it is emergent rather than authored: a Leech reaches for this when it is hurt and for something else when it is not. `cast_value` cannot see the condition and prices the healing whole, so it reads 6.75 where play reads between 4.35 and 6.75.

spell:hateful_sacrifice.name: Hateful Sacrifice
spell:hateful_sacrifice.intent: The largest single hit in the game, and it costs the caster three health to throw. The sacrifice is the name of the spell and it is finally in it (ADR 0031): the legacy prototype paired a hit of 10 with `SelfDirect Health -4`, and only the first half survived the port.
keep: The heaviest single-target hit
It is paid in the caster's own health: that is the sacrifice the name promises
spell:hateful_sacrifice.note: The self-damage was restored when its tier opened, which `docs/domain/spells.md` said would happen -- 'Psycho Rush and Hateful Sacrifice are still halves of themselves, and are re-authored when their tier is opened'. Its old second keep said the energy price stood in for the missing recoil; the recoil is here, so the stand-in is gone. It read 10.00 a round to 7.33, just under the tier-3 band of 8 to 14, and that was accepted rather than compensated: `cast_value` charges the health in full, where a bot pays it only in the rounds where that health is what it had left. #246 has since made it 11 damage for three health, which reads 9.00, inside the band. Measured, 621 casts to 420.

spell:soul_devourer.name: Soul Devourer
spell:soul_devourer.intent: Parasite Jab grown up: the Leech takes what it hits, and this one takes two things. The health it drinks is the class signature the opener already has; the energy it tears out is this spell's own, the half the port dropped and ADR 0035 gave back.
keep: It takes from what it hits: the Leech's whole line does, and this is the large version
It takes energy, not only health: that is what makes it a Soul Devourer and not a bigger `parasite_jab`
Heavier than `parasite_jab` on every half -- the hit, the heal, and a drain the opener does not have -- or the opener is the better spell
spell:soul_devourer.note: It was the worst rate in the catalogue at 2.00 a round and cast zero times -- a node on the line rather than a spell, because the half that made it a Soul Devourer was dropped at the port. A caster heal of 5 stood in for that half and got it to 9.00 a round and 343 casts. The drain is now expressible (ADR 0035) and it came back where legacy had it, 2 energy off the target (tune run 9 has since taken it to 3, and the damage 5 to 6), with the caster heal down from 5 to 4: the heal no longer has to carry a theft it was never about. The drain is worth 0.90 in `cast_value` and that reading is wrong in a way worth saying out loud -- energy is priced at 0.3 a point (ADR 0037, 0.2 before it), and taking three off a creature does not cost it three points of anything, it costs it the cast it was saving for. Nothing in the scorers read a cast denied until ADR 0091: the agents now price a drain that leaves an enemy still to act unable to pay as a stun round, which is the lock players found, since no immunity follows it. `cast_value` reads a spell without a board and still prices it at the energy rate. The owner raised the cost 2 to **3** on 2026-10-02 so that the lock cannot be cast every round on the income of a round, and the cost bound starts at 3.

spell:shadowstep.name: Shadowstep
spell:shadowstep.intent: The Assassin's spender: Momentum banks energy for free, and this is where it goes. A strike that leaves its caster moving first next round, because the branch is about getting there first rather than hitting hardest -- the one-creature version of what Death Squad gives the whole team at tier 3.
keep: Tempo on the caster, never bleed: the heavy bleed is Mortal Wound's at tier 3
A tier-2 price, beside Enraged Charge rather than above it: part of its value is the initiative, not the hit
spell:shadowstep.note: Authored at 7.8 a round in the check-knobs reading; the reading cannot see the energy Momentum feeds it, and no evaluation has measured it yet.

spell:momentum.name: Momentum
spell:momentum.intent: The Assassin's free strike: a light hit that costs nothing and gathers energy as it lands. It is Wait with a blade in it -- the same activation and the same price, zero -- and where Wait only gathers, Momentum gathers and cuts. The owner asked for it on 2026-09-25 (journal): an attack that costs no energy, deals two or three and gives two or three back. It used to build energy over the next rounds (`EnergyRegeneration`), and no agent cast it: the top of that box was 2.40 a round against rivals at 7 and more.
keep: Free: it costs no energy, which is the whole point of the spell
An attack on one enemy, and the energy lands on its caster in the same cast
Small on both halves, a hit and an income, never a nuke: the Assassin's filler, not its finisher

spell:death_squad.name: Death Squad
spell:death_squad.intent: The whole squad moves first. One activation buys the team a round of haste, which is what legacy wrote and what ADR 0036 finally made sayable: the Assassin does not out-damage anyone, it gets there first.
keep: Team-wide, or it is one creature's initiative and the Assassin has no reason to own it
One round: haste that lasts is a stat change, not a play
No damage and no energy: it buys tempo and only tempo
spell:death_squad.note: It was **cast 0 times in 400 matches** and its own bounds reached 1.20 a round against a tier-3 band of 8 to 14, so `check-knobs` reported it as a spell no move could make a choice -- correctly, because the numbers were never what was wrong with it. Legacy gave the team +10 initiative and +100% critical for a round; neither was expressible, so it was substituted into the tempo it was meant to *buy*, one energy an ally, and energy was 0.2 a point at the time (0.3 since ADR 0037, which would have read 0.90 -- the same dead spell). As the haste it always was it reads **12.60**. The critical half is still out and is a different shape, not a mirror (ADR 0036). Measured, it goes **0 declarations to 182**, of which 162 land, and applies 288 hastes. But greedy takes it to a **0.333 win share over 36 sides** while the exploring agent reads **0.463 over 54** -- the signature of a spell the scorer overvalues rather than a bad spell, the same shape `infectious_blast` showed from the other side. `mortal_wound` drops 104 declarations to 69 beside it, so the class is being crowded out of its own win condition by its support spell. At an amount of 1 it reads 6.30, below the band, and only 12 sides pick it up -- too few to read, which is why 2 ships. What this really names is the initiative weight: ADR 0032 swept 2.1 on content whose only initiative effect was a *debuff on one enemy*, and this entry asked whether the same price holds for a *buff on three allies*. ADR 0037 re-swept it over eleven points on content that carries this spell, and 2.1 won again -- so the price survives the buff, though it is a narrow minimum rather than a flat step and the question is answered rather than closed. There is no duration knob, because the first keep above says one round and a knob that can spend it is not a bound on the spell, it is a way out of its own identity. The amount stops at 3, whose corner reads **18.90** -- above the band on purpose, so the tuner has somewhere to go, and not a target: initiative is the dearest weight *per point* at 2.1 -- kill at 5.0 and stun at 3.0 are larger numbers, but neither multiplies an authored amount -- which makes this the easiest spell in the catalogue to over-tune.

spell:mortal_wound.name: Mortal Wound
spell:mortal_wound.intent: The bleed that actually kills: a hit now and a heavier wound over the rounds that follow. It is the reason to fear the Assassin and the likeliest single cause of a match that runs away from the loser.
keep: More damage over time than up front
The catalogue's heaviest bleed

spell:adrenaline_tonic.name: Adrenaline Tonic
spell:adrenaline_tonic.intent: The Plague Doctor's stimulant: a point of energy for up to three allies, with a point of poison in the same dose. It is Noxious Cure's idea turned to energy -- the remedy that costs something -- and its point is where the energy goes, not how much: across three allies it nets the team what Wait would, so it never out-earns waiting, but it brings three creatures to their next threshold a round early.
keep: Never out-earns Wait: the energy it spreads, less its price, stays at or under the two Wait gives
Always poisons what it feeds: every ally it reaches takes the bleed
spell:adrenaline_tonic.note: Authored at -1.5 a round in the check-knobs reading, which prices the bleed on an ally as a cost at 0.8 and the energy at 0.3; the greedy agents are unlikely ever to cast it, so an evaluation will say little about it. A spell for human players until the energy weight says otherwise.

spell:noxious_cure.name: Noxious Cure
spell:noxious_cure.intent: The cure is noxious to the cured: the whole team is mended and the whole team is left open for having drunk it. Legacy stripped 2 defense from the allies it healed and ADR 0035 gave that stat back, so the bargain is now written in the currency it was written in. The bargain is the spell: without a cost it is a free team heal, and the Trickster is the class that makes you pay for things.
keep: Team-wide heal: it reaches the team or it is Rejuvenate
It always shreds the allies it heals: the price is paid by the cured, which is what makes it noxious
The shred runs out: a cure that costs the team its armour for good is not a cure
spell:noxious_cure.note: Sized against an initiative weight of 0.5, the bargain broke when ADR 0032 measured that weight at 2.1: a slow of 2 cost 4.2 an ally where the heal of 4 is worth 3.2, the cast read **-3.00 a round** -- worse than doing nothing -- and the price had to come down to a slow of 1 to be payable at all. The cost is now the shred legacy wrote, 2 defense for one round, and it is affordable in a way the substitution never was: defense is 0.65 a point, so the price is 1.30 an ally against a heal worth 3.20. That is the ADR's point in one line -- the spell did not need smaller numbers, it needed the right stat. The bounds stay where they were rebuilt, and the amount reaches 3 because the shred has room the slow did not. Two readings the numbers still hide. `ActionScorer`'s `HealTerms` counts only the health an ally is missing, so on a whole team this is worth nothing and it is never a free cast. And the debuff is a **cost** although it is written like any other effect -- the targeting origin is what says so, and both `cast_value` and `dominates` had to be taught it: read unsigned, shredding the allies you heal makes this spell read as strictly better than a plain heal of the same size.

spell:tranquilizer_dart.name: Tranquilizer Dart
spell:tranquilizer_dart.intent: The cheap stun: a stolen activation for half what Crushing Stomp asks, and almost nothing else. The Trickster buys the tempo the Warlord pays full price for, and pays for it in damage.
keep: Cheaper than Crushing Stomp and weaker for it
The stun is the spell: the damage is a rounding error, not a second half
spell:tranquilizer_dart.note: It was **1 declaration in 400 matches** -- and legacy is not what went wrong with it. The port is faithful (3 energy, 3 damage, a one-round stun) and so was the relationship it was built on: legacy Crushing Stomp is 4 energy, 6 damage, and a stun of **one round**. The second round is this catalogue's, added in the Warlord pass along with damage 6 to 7 and a critical chance of 0.75, and it turned the cheap stun into a strictly worse expensive one -- 75% of the price for 44% of the reading. Nothing caught it: `outclassed` compares a spell's *ceiling* against a rival's *current* value, and this spell's ceiling sat just under `ice_spear`'s, so the check named the Wizard and never mentioned the Warlord. The fix is this spell's own intent, applied: price **2**, damage 3 to **2**, stun to **2 rounds**. 4.00 a round to 8.00, inside the band and still under `crushing_stomp`'s 9.12 -- cheaper and weaker, which is the first keep, while buying tempo at half the Warlord's price, which is the sentence the intent has always carried. Measured: 1 declaration to **78**, 72 stuns landed, and `crushing_stomp` unmoved at 93.1% over 99. Greedy wins 0.387 of the sides that declare it against the exploring agent's **0.659 over 44** -- greedy under-plays it, which is `death_squad`'s split read the other way round. The `check-knobs` finding of the time -- a ceiling of 10.00 against `ice_spear` at 10.20 -- is gone: the dart's bounds now reach 11.60 and `ice_spear` reads 9.00. The owner set the stun back to **one round** on 2026-09-30, keeping the price at 2, and gave the dart a poison: a bleed of 1 for 2 rounds, because Ice Spear, already at two energy, became a one-round stun with more damage in the same change and would otherwise have strictly dominated it. 8.00 a round to 6.60; the 1-in-400 of legacy was a 3-energy dart; this one, measured on `9659f610`, is cast 9 times on the confirmation seeds' exploring run, which keeps Blightweaver the least bought tier-3 package.

spell:infectious_blast.name: Infectious Blast
spell:infectious_blast.intent: A plague cloud: one energy to strip the armour off the whole enemy team for good, with a little damage as it lands. It is what the rest of the board hits through, so what it is worth depends on who is casting beside it.
keep: Control first: the shred is the spell, and the damage stays a sting on each target, two at most, even where three of them add up
The cheapest thing that touches all three enemies
The shred is permanent: the Trickster takes something off the board rather than borrowing it
spell:infectious_blast.note: It carried the substitution ADR 0035 removed, and it carried it at the wrong price: rendered as tempo it read **25.20 a round**, the largest number in the catalogue, and `revenant_guards` and `death_squad` were both reported as having no bounds that could make them a choice beside it. As the defense debuff it always was it read 11.70, inside the tier-3 band; #246 raised the debuff to 3 and #247 added 2 damage, and it reads **23.55** today, the largest number in the catalogue again. The `revenant_guards` finding went away without either spell moving, and `death_squad` is no longer reported at all; today `check-knobs` reports `crazed_specter`, `tornado` and `toxic_waves` against this spell's 23.55, each with a ceiling under it. The duration knob went with the substitution -- the debuff is permanent, and a permanent duration is not a number the tuner can turn.

spell:lightning_bolt.name: Lightning Bolt
spell:lightning_bolt.intent: The Sorcerer's bread and butter: a modest hit that crits one time in two. It is the caster's mirror of Pummel and the spell every Sorcerer branch gets compared against.
keep: The class's baseline attack: everything deeper in the tree must beat it
spell:lightning_bolt.note: Its price is the open question of this catalogue, so the cost bound is wider than most. At two energy it takes 85% of the landed casts on the core content; at three it takes 36%, matches run 9.5 rounds instead of 8.1, and the objective falls from 104.1 to 19.4. Nothing says three is the end of that curve, so the knob reaches four. Its critical chance was listed here as its identity until a measurement showed the identity does not distinguish it: Pummel carried the same 0.667 then (0.767 today, against this spell's 0.5), and a critical multiplies base damage, so at equal rates it widens the gap it is supposed to close. Against a Pummel at 3 damage, dropping this spell's chance to 0.417 leaves Pummel 448 landed casts of about 5900, 0.317 leaves it 649, and one in six flips the catalogue: Pummel 4986, this spell 754, and eight spells cast instead of seven. The cost is length -- 7.6, 9.2 and 11.3 rounds, with the round-cap share 0.000, 0.045 and 0.100 against a band of 0.05 -- so the objective has a real trade to arbitrate, and none of that range was reachable at a floor of 0.4. What makes this a Sorcerer spell rather than a Brawler one is deliberately left unstated: the critical chance no longer says it, and the answer is a design decision rather than a bound. On 2026-09-30 the owner took the critical chance from 0.617 to **0.5**: on content `c8d39320`, score-content 7.53 to 5.26 on the benchmark seeds and 10.91 to 9.02 on the confirmation seeds, with Greedy still beating Random every time and the best exploiter slowed from 14.5 rounds to 12.2. At 0.4 and below the spell falls from about 6,000 casts to 1,000 behind Heavy Strike, Greedy's edge over Random drops to 0.88, and the exploiter closes in 8.4 rounds: a line worth understanding before going there.

spell:rejuvenate.name: Rejuvenate
spell:rejuvenate.intent: The Sorcerer's first heal and the reason a Sorcerer team can outlast a Brawler team: 4 health for two energy, the price the healing line is measured from. Healing Screech, Restorative Gush and Noxious Cure cost the same and have to justify it by healing more; Soothing Chant costs one by healing less, over time.
keep: No instant heal costs less: only `soothing_chant` is cheaper, and it heals over time
Single target
spell:rejuvenate.note: Its critical chance became a live number with ADR 0033 -- the multiplier reaches a direct heal -- so the 0.17 it had been carrying as decoration became worth 0.68 of expected healing, and it is a knob; tune run 6 took it to 0.22, 0.88 today. The heal that sets the price of the line is exactly the spell whose expected size should be tunable without moving the number a reader sees.

spell:frostbite.name: Frostbite
spell:frostbite.intent: The Elementalist's spare-energy spell: one point is what Meteor leaves behind on an income of two, and this spends it. A light chill that slows its target for a round -- the cold before the ice: Ice Spear freezes outright at tier 3.
keep: One energy: it exists to spend what Meteor leaves over
A slow, not a nuke: the damage stays small and the chill lasts one round
spell:frostbite.note: Authored at 7.0 a round in the check-knobs reading, most of it the initiative debuff at the 2.1 weight -- the only initiative slow in the Wizard line now that Ice Spear stuns instead. No evaluation has measured it yet.

spell:meteor.name: Meteor
spell:meteor.intent: The Wizard's sweep, and the spell that says what reach costs: each enemy takes less than one of them would take from a single-target spell of the same depth, and the whole line reads 7.00 a round, under the tier-2 hits beside it (Enraged Charge and Shield Bash at 8.40, Protective Slam at 9.02). It is the only sweep in a class whose other three spells each strike one target, so it is the one that has to make the trade legible -- a sweep that hit as hard per target as a bolt would simply be a bolt that hits three.
keep: Reaches three enemies
Each of them takes less than a single-target spell of its tier deals: reach is paid for per target
The strongest thing in its tier, but by a step and not by half again
spell:meteor.note: Its bounds used to defer to Tornado -- 'these two are priced against each other or one of them is dead content' -- and Tornado was a tier deeper and disabled then, so this spell was deferring its numbers to one nobody could cast while it became the ceiling of its own tier. Read per round, four damage on three targets was 12.00 against `enraged_charge`'s 8.40, 43% clear of everything; three was 9.00, a step ahead rather than a different game; reworked since to 2 damage and a one-round bleed, it reads 7.00, now behind `enraged_charge`'s 8.40. The damage floor drops to 2 so a real per-target discount is reachable, and the cap to 4, `lightning_bolt`'s own damage on one, so its hit per target can never exceed the bolt's. Tornado is enabled now, at tier 3 in Ravager, so the comparison is back: Tornado reads 13.80 a round against this spell's 7.00, a comparison between two sweeps rather than a reason to leave this one unpriced.

spell:engulfing_flames.name: Engulfing Flames
spell:engulfing_flames.intent: The clean nuke. The catalogue holds three big single-target hits at three energy and this is the only one that costs its caster nothing -- Psycho Rush leaves the Berserker open for a round, Hateful Sacrifice takes three of the Leech's own health, and the Wizard simply casts.
keep: No caster effect: what separates it from Psycho Rush and Hateful Sacrifice is that it pays nothing
It pays for that once, in critical chance, and not twice
The Wizard's single-target answer to its own sweep
spell:engulfing_flames.note: Its old intent read 'Psycho Rush in a robe: the same cost, the same damage, the same critical chance and the same targeting', and its first keep was 'must stop being a copy of Psycho Rush'. That was settled by the **Berserker** pass, not by this spell: Psycho Rush now carries 10 damage, a chance of 0.5 and a recoil on its own caster. The claim is withdrawn. What was left was a spell paying twice for the one thing that makes it itself -- 9 damage *and* a chance of 0.33 against the other two's 10 and 0.5, for the privilege of costing nothing. Damage goes to **10**, so the discount is taken once, in the chance alone: 7.98 a round to **8.87**, between Psycho Rush's 9.13 and Hateful Sacrifice's 7.33 at the time; #246 has since raised Hateful Sacrifice to 9.00, so this spell now reads the lowest of the three. The `check-knobs` finding against `ice_spear` was **twice an artifact**: `cast_value` has no kill term, which is what a nuke is for, and it priced `ice_spear`'s slow at 2.1 a point, which was 41% of that spell's reading. The finding stays, now against `soul_devourer` at 10.10 over this spell's ceiling of 10.00, and the missing kill term still applies. Measured on content `eca50723`, after [ADR 0042](../../docs/adr/0042-a-creature-has-no-base-critical-chance.md) took the crit floor off every cast, the gap is **wider than when this note was written**, not narrower: the two win **71.2% and 44.1%** of the sides that declare them, where they read 44.4% and 49.0% before, and this one now takes 690 damage to its 653 in **77 landed casts against 127**. spell:ice_spear.note: Its bounds are narrowed, not its numbers. The slow could reach 3 points over 2 rounds, which at 2.1 a point is a tempo term of 12.60 against the 4.20 it carried then (it carries no slow today, a one-round stun worth 3.00 instead) -- a ceiling of **20.60**, the third largest in the catalogue, on the one weight three entries in a row have now called suspect. The duration knob went first because it contradicts the second keep above: 'it wins the next round' is one round, and a knob that can spend two is not a bound on the spell but a way out of its own identity -- the same thing `tranquilizer_dart`'s duration knob was. The amount stopped at 2, which is where the content sat when these bounds were drawn; that knob went with the slow. Ceiling 20.60 to **12.20**; nothing a build reads has moved. This spell was also the bar two others could not clear (`engulfing_flames` at a ceiling of 10.00, `tranquilizer_dart` at 10.00, against its 10.20), and **41% of its 10.20 was that slow**. It read 49.0% against `engulfing_flames`'s 44.4% while doing less than half the damage, so the gap the check reported was already far larger than the gap that was there. On content `eca50723`, after [ADR 0042](../../docs/adr/0042-a-creature-has-no-base-critical-chance.md) took the crit floor off every cast, that reading has **inverted rather than narrowed**: this spell wins **44.1%** of the sides that declare it against `engulfing_flames`'s **71.2%**, and the damage it was losing on it has caught up only by casting far more often -- 653 to 690, in **127 landed casts against 77**. Read that as an argument about `cast_value`, which has no kill term, and not as a reason to move these bounds: lowering a spell already at 44.1% to satisfy a number that is wrong about it fixes the report and not the game. Tune run 9 then moved it anyway, and in the shape that argument asks for rather than the one tune 8 took: the slow 2 points to **1**, the cost back 3 to **2**. On content `7e199df4` it carries **8.10**, a quarter of it the slow, and it is no longer the bar for anything -- `check-knobs` named `soul_devourer` at 10.10 for both spells that used to be measured against this one, and today names it for `engulfing_flames` and `psycho_rush`; `tranquilizer_dart` is no longer reported. Raising them is paid in the Necromancer's own health, so the class opens on a bargain rather than on a blow -- patience bought with life. spell:summon_minions.note: Two traits, and they are the design: it defers all of its damage, and it charges its caster health (ADR 0031) -- no longer alone in either, since `latch` defers its damage too and `bone_ward`, `crazed_specter`, `revenant_guards`, `reckless_swing` and `hateful_sacrifice` charge health. It used to be `EnergyGain 3` for 2, an approximation of the minions the two spells behind it spent -- and ADR 0020 named it as one of the two candidates for `EnergyRegeneration`. That nomination is declined here, with a measurement: energy was 0.2 a point then and is 0.3 since ADR 0037, so an energy spell tops out around 1.60 an activation and 2.40 today, against an attack's 6 and up either way, and `momentum` was measured cast 0 times at `explore:0.2` and 8 at `explore:0.5` after being given exactly that treatment. spell:revenant_guards.name: Revenant Guards
spell:revenant_guards.intent: Thundering Seal for the whole team, paid in the Necromancer's own blood: permanent defense on three allies at once, and four health off whoever raised them. It is the willingness to pay its parent names, spent on the team instead of on the enemy.

spell:revenant_guards.note: Its second keep was **false**. It asked to be priced above `thundering_seal` while both cost two energy, so the team-wide version simply replaced the single-target one -- 15.60 a round against 9.75, the second-largest reading in the catalogue and above a tier-3 band of 8 to 14. Legacy says why: `MinionsCost = 1`, a second currency the port dropped for this spell and for `crazed_specter` (`docs/domain/spells.md`, 'Minions'). `summon_minions` already settled what a minion costs when it charged the summoner's own health, so spending one costs the same: **4 health on the caster**, as a one-round `Bleed` (ADR 0031). 15.60 to **12.40**, inside the band, and the keep is true in the currency that matters -- `thundering_seal` costs two energy and nothing else, this cost two energy *and* four health. No energy price moved then; tune run 9 has since raised this one to three. The price is a bleed and not a `Damage` because **this spell would otherwise pay its own price down**: `Ally` targeting includes the caster (`TargetingRules`), so every cast permanently armours the summoner, and `ResolutionRules` reduces a caster `Damage` by that armour -- 3 health on the first cast, 1 on the second, 0 on the third. A bleed tick ignores defense (ADR 0019), so the toll is the same every time. `ResolutionRulesTests` pins the difference. Its critical chance is still not a knob after ADR 0033: the multiplier reaches a target's damage and direct heal, and this spell does neither -- it is the one shape the rule leaves out.

Legacy carries `MinionsCost = 1` on it, dropped at the port, and `summon_minions` already fixed what a minion costs by charging the summoner's health.
